audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Grant 2013 §5/§6; Hale 1890 dictionary introduction and Grammar p. 12) are verbatim in the copies we hold at the B-corrected locators. (2) Deciding source: an APiCS survey chapter (2013, specialist author, publisher text) plus an 1890 manual that marks accent per entry; not a grammar or phonology study, but for this extinct-as-pidgin languoid no dedicated stress study exists. Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description grammar (Robertson 2011, 309 pp) was downloaded and read: it says outright that stress/intonation data are absent from the Kamloops corpus, so the best available grammar is silent and cannot improve the record. Thomason 2004 (downloaded) and Demers et al. 1871 (downloaded scanned) are silent. The Grand Ronde materials already held under chin1272 (Zenk 1993: 'usual first-syllable stress' with variable stress and initial-stress alternants for French-derived items; Robertson 20

sources.quote: 'KCW suprasegmentals such as stress, intonation, and juncture are essentially absent from my corpus. No KCW material from Indigenous writers or Le Jeune indicates prosody in an interpretable way.' Only datum: emphatic lengthening of the stressed vowel, [sajá::] 'way far away' (cf. pan-CW sajá 'far').

sources.note: The fullest modern statement of CW stress ('Zenk's Law': trochaic/initial main stress, alternating secondaries, French la-/li- nouns final or variable); strictly describes the Grand Ronde creolized variety (chin1272) but is the reference Grant's APiCS chapter draws on and would let the record state the default and the exception class precisely.

sources.note: Earliest fieldwork-based linguistic description of CJ; per Robertson (chinookjargon.com 2018) it treats stress on p. 32. Our record rests on a 2013 survey sentence plus an 1890 manual; Jacobs is the primary linguistic statement for the pidgin era and could turn the hedged 'generally penultimate' into a firmer default-initial/penult-with-lexical-exceptions reading.
